standard.title: Recognise and compare target language and English features
standard.description: recognise familiar target language features and compare with those of English, in known contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can notice structural similarities and differences between the target language and English including shared vocabulary, plurals and structural patterns (AC9LS2U03). They have not yet built metalanguage for grammar comparison or recognised systematic vocabulary pattern connections.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise familiar target language features and compare them with English — using grammatical metalanguage and comparing text types, conventions and vocabulary patterns.

nodes.label: Grammatical metalanguage for comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use grammatical metalanguage to compare target language and English features — naming and discussing grammar concepts in both languages.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least four metalanguage terms accurately to describe target language grammatical features.
nodes.typical_width: Build and apply metalanguage for grammar discussion; compare grammatical terms across the target language and English; use metalanguage to discuss and compare specific features; recognise systematic vocabulary pattern connections between the two languages.
wider: Apply a systematic vocabulary pattern to predict the English equivalent of unfamiliar target language words — test predictions and identify exceptions
Produce a bilingual grammar glossary for at least six terms — defining each in both languages with an example sentence
nodes.hinge_reason: Grammatical metalanguage is the shared vocabulary for all explicit language comparison and analysis work. Students who lack this vocabulary cannot participate in the increasingly analytical grammar and text discussions that build from subsequent bands.

response_modes.reason: Metalanguage accuracy requires repeated application across varied grammar contexts. Students need to use terms consistently across multiple examples before they become reliable analytical tools.

success_criteria: Uses at least four metalanguage terms correctly in describing target language grammatical features
Identifies at least two target language-English vocabulary pattern connections

nodes.label: Comparing text types and conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare features of similar text types in the target language and English — identifying similarities and differences in language use, word order, formality and conventions.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two features of the same text type in the target language and English — identifying one similarity and one difference.
nodes.typical_width: Compare target language and English text types — cards, games, menus, invitations, stories; discuss similarities and differences in word order, expression, formality and conventions; recognise formality variation within text types; apply punctuation knowledge across languages.
wider: Find an authentic target language text of a familiar type and compare it line by line with an English equivalent — annotate every difference noticed
Explain to a target language community member how an Australian English version of a familiar text type differs from the target language version

response_modes.reason: Text-type comparison develops through encountering varied text types across both languages. Each new text-type comparison reveals different dimensions of the language relationship.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Text-type comparison using authentic target language materials connects metalinguistic analysis to genuine cultural documents — enabling students to engage with authentic texts as comparison objects.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between a target language and English version of the same text type
Uses at least two metalanguage terms when describing the comparison
